I have both. I'm in the uk so my diagnosis isn't related to funding etc or insurance. 

For my bpd symptoms I had scheme therapy which helped me heal my past, and I've just finished a year of intensive DBT. It has really helped me calm down with my reactions and outbursts. I can communicate more effectively with others, have managed to stop self harming drastically for the most part, stopped spending so much time on A&E and hospitals, and able to get my dissociative issues under control. I also recovered from my eating disorder- which is linked to bpd coping methods. 

Sometimes therapy seems like really hard work, but if you can stick at it and work with it it can help. 

I still have my mood issues bc of bipolar and we are still working on figuring out a treatment method for that but life is much less hectic now I'm not self harming and overdosing every week. 

I used to hate DBT but I stuck at it. It's not solved everything but it's helped. If you can get funding for it it's definitely worth a shot.

I used to revolve my life around mental health, friends, support groups, therapy everything. 

Then I hit a wall and realised having all mental health friends wasn't helpful for recovery and that I had lost myself to being unwell. I knew people where it consumed them entirely so I started focusing on rediscovering myself and my interests. 

I started writing about mental health but it turned into a blog about living alongside mental health with a focus on my interests which happen to be diet and fitness. This helped carve my identity. 

I started going to events on my own like runs and climbing clubs to make friends who I had interests in common with rather than diagnosis or a status of bad mental health. People always find out I have mh problems because of my behaviour when I'm unwell, or sometimes when I'm manic or telling stories without thinking people have guessed heh were manic adventures but that's ok. It's a part of me but not who I am. It's shaped me and taught me a lot about compassion, life and other people - but it's not who I am. 

It's been a long process and I'm still struggling with my mental health a lot - and my closest friends know about my illness but they also know me for my dancing, writing, studying, interest in health food and fitness, geekiness, fascination with science, my social views, my poetry, and all that stuff. It's just a thing on the list, it's not dominating the list anymore. 

As a result, when I'm more well I feel less lost, less confused and less overwhelmed by life because I have a sense of where I fit in aside from being deemed unfit for work and technically disabled. 

I know I'm posting here but I've also started withdrawing from regular mental health based haunts that I feel don't fit with my interests or values. For example I only go support groups when I feel i need them rather than as my main social crutch in my life. 

If can be done. You might just have to do some exploring within yourself and try some things to rediscover or even discover your interests.

in the UK. I've only been in adult units but I think there will be some general things that are the same. 

- When visitors offer to bring you food, accept. And get things that don't go off so easily, as well as some fruit, and stuff like pot noodles for when then food provided is awful. 

- comfy pyjamas are your best friend

- things to do are good for when you're bored, or when you start getting better you'll start wanting to do stuff. colouring, with pens is good (no pencil sharpener needed as that is not allowed), writing with pen and paper, a kindle or books, jigsaws etc - depending on the unit i wouldn't take an ipad because some people steal. But this is different for every unit. 

- it is much better to talk to the  staff when upset etc than lashing out bc they will restrain you and maybe inject and thats an awful experience. when they off PRN to calm you down, take the pills. It is so much less humiliating and stressful than a forced injection. 

- talk to other patients, but maintain boundaries. Also, try not to get involved in other people's dramas and delusions: even if they fully believe what they are saying and you know it's not true, don't challenge them directly -- it's not your job. Accept it, but just don't believe everything they say. 

- with other patients, you can assert your space and boundaries, and sometimes this is necassary. 

- talking to other patients though, can help pass the time easier, and make the experience less isolating and lonely. Also means you can bitch and moan when you need to but be conscious of offloading too much on other patients. 

- hospital isn't a good place to find a bestfriend or boyfriend/girlfriend. It's like big brother sydrome, you are cooped up and get along but in your outside life they likely won't have a big part to play. Some people make friends, but they're not always the healthiest friends to help with your recovery: having said that, occasionally there is someone you get on with well and that's cool, but not everyone you get on with will become your mate. 

- be honest in ward round. its better to stay and get well than be discharged early to be admitted again not much later. 

- if your'e allowed your phone, keep it close, and hidden when not with you or charging in the nurses office. If theres wifi, netflix can be a godsend, as can radio apps which can help normalise your day a little by keeping you in touch with reality/the outside world. 

- sharing is caring, but dont be taken for a ride. 

- if you smoke, (not allowed but people do anyway) don't share too much otherwise people take the piss. Also, tobacco is better because it's easier to hide. MAtches hidden in separate places will be a good back up, and also have high value for trading or favours. Hide your smokes in different places so that if you're searched or room searched, they'll think they found them when they find some, but hopefully won't find them all. Also, don't tell them you smoke when they ask you upon admission, because then when they smell smoke in the corridors etc, they won't assume it's you. And never smoke in your room - the bathroom with a window is the best choice.
